# Education in New Zealand
New Zealand’s education system has its roots in Māori traditional knowledge transfer before European-style schooling was introduced in the early 19th century by missionaries. A national, free, compulsory, and secular education system was established in 1878, influenced by Victorian ideals. Early childhood education includes centre-based (kindergarten, licensed centres) and whānau-led services, regulated by the Ministry of Education but typically not government-owned. Primary and secondary education is free for all citizens and permanent residents from age 5 to 19, with compulsory attendance between ages 6 and 16. Schooling is divided into 13 year levels, with primary education covering Years 1–8 (including intermediate years 7 and 8) and secondary education covering Years 9–13. The school year runs from late January to mid-December with four terms.
The national curriculum, which public and state-integrated schools must follow, includes eight learning areas such as English or Māori language, mathematics, science, and social sciences. Students work toward the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) in senior years, with some schools offering Cambridge International or International Baccalaureate qualifications. Types of schools include state (government-funded), state-integrated (former private with special character, charging "attendance dues"), and private schools (tuition-based). Approximately 85% of students attend state schools. Enrolment schemes regulate admissions based on geographic zones to manage school roll sizes.
Māori language education has experienced a revival with immersion schools (Kura Kaupapa Māori) and Māori-medium programs alongside English-medium schooling, though enrolment percentages have declined slightly since 2004. Māori language education is recognized under the Treaty of Waitangi and supported by legislation.
Tertiary education encompasses a broad range of post-school education regulated by the New Zealand Qualifications Framework, including informal courses, vocational training, undergraduate degrees, and postgraduate study. Primary and secondary schools receive government funding per student, adjusted for school size and socio-economic decile, supplemented by voluntary donations; state-integrated schools charge compulsory attendance dues. Tertiary education funding combines government subsidies and student fees, with access to student loans and allowances. While New Zealand ranks highly in some global education assessments, concerns remain about declining standards in numeracy and science in recent years, with ongoing efforts to improve educational outcomes for Māori and Pacific Island students to achieve parity with Pākehā students. Bullying is a notable issue, prompting government initiatives for anti-bullying policies and programs.
